No MSAA. Dots and layers draw from static buffers; nothing runs per frame on the CPU.

# Photo prints A photograph printed whole by a shader in the page's ink on its own sheet: a halftone, an engraving or a dither. Hover (a tap on a phone) shows the photograph itself under the print. A print is one crafted moment on a page, never the way a page shows its photographs. | Object | Looks like | Hover | |---|---|---| | `photo-halftone` | a one-ink halftone: round dots on a 45° screen, clean paper in the light, solid ink in the deepest shadow | a loupe (round lens, hairline rim, soft shadow) shows the photograph in its own colours | | `photo-engraving` | an engraved plate: diagonal lines that swell in shadow and bend over the forms, over a light wash of the photograph's colour | the lines part around the cursor and the photograph shows through | | `photo-dither` | a three-colour grain: the photograph's deepest and most colourful colours on the paper | the photograph develops through the grain in a soft circle | Each folder's `demo.html` (served over http) shows it in the light, dark and colour palettes. `meta.json` lists its params, touch behaviour, fallback and cost. ## Where a print goes, and where not - **Yes:** one moment on a software, AI, design-tool or gaming page: the page's one photograph band, or a feature tile whose subject is the photograph (an imaging or design tool printing a picture, `tint: 1` for the brand's ink). One print per page; a row of three only on a page about prints. - **Never** over the hero photograph or a section's main photograph (`references/photos.md`): a print there reads as broken or low-resolution. Never on a café, guesthouse, shop or other local business page: those show their photographs plain. - **Never** a caption under it that explains the effect, and no note that it is a print. ## The photograph The client's own photograph first. Else one from the vetted library that prints well (one clear subject, a plain ground, clear light): ```bash node /scripts/photos.mjs list --trade office --json # entries with "prints": true node /scripts/photos.mjs fetch --out . # the files, credits.json and the ``` On a dark page pick a darker photograph (`"tone": "dark"` or `"mid"`): a pale one prints as a large light plate there. ## Mount Paste the `` that `photos.mjs fetch` prints into the frame. The print reads that picture (the largest `srcset` size), keeps its `alt`, and takes its `object-position` as the subject's place. ```html
``` - The frame needs a size (an `aspect-ratio` or a height). The print fills it, prints on the page's `--surface` so the frame reads as a sheet (`ground: 0` prints on `--bg`), and follows the page's palette (`ctrl.setPalette(fx.readPalette(el))` after a palette switch). - `focusX`/`focusY` (0..1) override the ``'s `object-position`. - The print is there from its first frame: no entry, no dissolve, nothing moves at rest. - A small UI card may sit on a corner of the frame (`cards.md`), never over the subject; never text over the print. ## Credit Credits go in the footer's one credits line, never under the print. A printed photograph counts as adapted: ```bash node /scripts/photos.mjs credits --out . --adapted ``` For a photograph that did not come through `photos.mjs`, `creditsBlock(entries, { adapted: [id] })` in `photo.js` writes the same footer block from `{ id, by, page, licence, licenceUrl, source }` (one line, "Photographs via ...", that opens the list). The client's own photograph needs none. ## When it cannot draw Before the first frame, while the canvas is released off screen, and whenever WebGL is missing, the shader fails to compile or link, or the photograph's host sends no CORS headers, the photograph itself shows, greyed into the palette: a still picture, never an empty frame. The runtime also refuses a shader that uses a GLSL ES reserved word (`flat`, `smooth`, `sample`, `filter`, `input`...) and shows the still, because a laptop's GPU rejects what CPU WebGL (SwiftShader) compiles. `glslLint(src)` and `photoShader(object)` in `photo.js` check a shader from Node. ## Cost One canvas and one WebGL context per print, paused off screen and with the tab hidden, released 1.5 s after it leaves the screen. At most 3 prints hold a context; a fourth waits (showing its still) until one leaves, and a frame scrolling away gives way to one coming in. Count them with the page's other WebGL effects (keep a page to 3 live contexts). The halftone and engraving render up to 2 canvas px per CSS px so dots and lines stay sharp; every print stays under 1.5 MP of canvas. Each pixel reads the photograph 2 to 5 times from its mipmaps; no loops.

# Product render (`assets/objects/product-render`) A studio render of **any physical product**, composed from a short JSON spec: a list of parts with sizes and positions in the product's own units. `build.js` turns the spec into a model and `_print-core/print3d.js` renders it: real materials (painted metal, alloy, chrome, rubber, wood, fabric, leather, plastic, a light), soft studio light with soft shadows, a softbox in glossy parts, a floor shadow, the page's accent on the parts that ask for it. It sways slowly as a turntable, or holds still; a lamp switches on and off on a click; a robot's joints move. Use it when the **brief asks for 3D or a render** (a configurator, a product that exists only as a model): the render is the product's picture, in the hero and the statement. A product without photographs and without that ask is shown in photographs, its own or stand-ins (`references/photos.md`). Never for a product that has photographs, never on a place page, never captioned, never a product of another kind. One product render a page. ## Mount: the product at anchor scale ```html
``` The frame is the picture: the product's own bounds fill a share of it (the tighter way, width or height) and it stands on the page's ground with its floor shadow, transparent round it: **no panel, no grey box**. Give the frame its size (a hero column as tall as the screen, a full-width stage, a tile); the product fills it. | attribute | | |---|---| | `data-product-place` | `hero` 0.88, `stage` 0.86, `tile` 0.84, `card` 0.9 of the frame (`legacy`: the old turntable right of the words) | | `data-product-view` | `three-quarter` (default), then only the views the spec lists in `supports` (`side`, `front`, `top`, a close-up of its own such as `detail-saddle`); `product.views` lists them; any other (the bike's `top`) throws and the frame carries `data-product-error`; or `detail:` | | `data-product-scene` | a scene of the spec: the product loaded or in use (`loaded`, `desk`, `work`) | | `data-product-color` | a colourway id of the spec (`spec.colors`); default its first | | `data-product-mode` | `auto` (default): the still make-posters made, else the turn, else one frame rendered here; `image`, `still`, `live` force one | | `data-product-fill` | 0.3-1.2, over the place's share | | `data-product-params` | `{"turn":1}` asks for the live turn; `{"x":0.1,"y":-0.05}` moves it; `{"step":0}` a lamp off | | `data-product-palette` | `{ bg, surface, ink, accent }`; else the page's tokens `--bg`, `--ink`, `--accent` | **Each section a different view.** A product page shows the product big, whole in three sections at most, and never the same view twice: the widest view in the hero (a bike's `side`; a lamp's or an arm's `three-quarter`), another angle by the specs, a close-up on the part a section talks about, the loaded scene where the copy promises what it carries. Every promise in a headline is shown in a picture (a child seat with its belts, the crates, a lamp's light on the desk). **A close-up** (`detail-*`, `detail:`) frames the named parts and centres them on the frame (their box, `focus` in the manifest, fills the place's share); the rest of the product runs off the frame's edges (the frame clips it), never a hard cut inside it. So that holds in a wide tile too, a close-up's shot is made wide enough (`cover`, default 2: a frame up to twice as wide as tall, 1 : 1.25 tall) with the product running on past the parts as far as it goes, and its still is cropped evenly round the parts' centre, never to the product's own box. **Colour from an order card.** A swatch drives the frames it names, no script needed: ```html ``` On click (a button: `aria-pressed` is kept, one pressed per group) or change (an input), the named frames (default: every frame whose spec has that colourway) set `data-product-color` and swap to that colour's still. Setting `data-product-color`, `-view` or `-scene` on a mounted frame does the same, and so does an event: `el.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('product:set', { detail: { color: 'red', view: 'side' } }))`, or on `document` with `detail.target` a selector. **What a frame tells** (for checkers and tests): `data-product-mode`, `data-product-state` (`image` | `still` | `live` | `poster`), `data-product-view`, `data-product-color-shown`; the picture is `img.product-render__img`; `window.__tpProduct` = `{ stills, images, live, freed }`. In `image` mode the page holds no canvas and no WebGL context; a `still` renders once, keeps an ``, frees its context and removes its canvases; only `live` keeps a context (and counts in `window.__tpGl`). A product page uses the stills (the default once make-posters has run). A `still` is measured (its opaque pixels, and a close-up's parts) and placed by the same layout as a poster still, so it fills its place's share exactly (tile .84) and is centred. Script: `import { loadProduct } from '.../product-render/build.js'; const p = await loadProduct(url); const ctrl = p.mount(el, { place: 'stage', view: 'side', scene, color, mode });` The controller: `setColor(id)`, `setView(v)`, `setScene(s)`, `ready()`, `pause()`, `resume()`, `step(on)`, `set(params)`, `setPalette(p | null)`, `destroy()`. `auto.js` exports `products` (frame to controller) and `ready`. `views.html` beside this file is the worked example (every view, a scene per spec, two colour switches, one `still` mount). ## Stills and posters: run this after every change to a spec ``` node assets/objects/product-render/make-posters.mjs path/to/spec.json --profile [--port 5905] [--variants side,detail-saddle,three-quarter+loaded] [--grounds light,dark] [--px 1100] [--timeout 9] [--quiet] [--legacy] node assets/objects/product-render/make-posters.mjs --check path/to/spec.json (spec, views, scenes and shaders only) ``` It checks the spec (unknown parts, props or materials, a part a view or scene names that is not there, too many parts, shader words a laptop GPU rejects), then renders in a headless, software-rendered Chrome (its own profile, closed by its own PID, never port 3000) every variant in `spec.make.variants` (`view` or `view+scene`) on each ground in `spec.make.grounds`, and writes beside the spec: `stills/--[-dark].webp` and `-half.webp` (one still per colourway, transparent, cropped to the product and its shadow), `-.fallback-render[-dark].png` (the live render's poster) and `.stills.json` (what was made, where the product and a close-up's framed parts sit, and which sides a close-up cuts). A colourway costs no render: the accent part is lit again in each colour. Each variant is written as soon as it is made; a CPU takes one to four minutes a variant for 60-90 parts, so pass `--variants` a few at a time. `--legacy` also writes the turntable's four posters. A view with no still renders itself once on the page (`still` mode) and frees its context. ## The spec ```json { "id": "city-bike", "name": "City bicycle", "label": "A city bicycle with a front basket", "units": "m", "angle": -34, "turn": { "mode": "sway", "amp": 22, "period": 24 }, "materials": { "frame": { "kind": "paint", "color": "accent", "finish": "gloss" } }, "parts": [ { "type": "wheel", "at": [-0.53, 0.35, 0], "r": 0.35, "spokes": 36, "wall": "#c7a57a" }, { "type": "tube", "from": [-0.07, 0.29, 0], "to": [-0.23, 0.81, 0], "r": 0.017, "mat": "frame", "blend": 0.01 } ] } ``` Axes: **x forward** (the product's front), **y up**, **z across** (toward the viewer at angle 0). Any unit; the model is scaled so its largest side is one unit and set on the floor at its lowest point. Model the product from its real measurements: proportions are most of what makes it read as a render. | key | what | |---|---| | `id`, `name`, `label` | the label is what a screen reader hears ("A desk lamp, switched on") | | `poster` | the posters' file name (default the id) | | `angle` | its turn at rest and in the still, degrees (default -32: a three-quarter view) | | `turn` | `{ "mode": "sway", "amp": 26, "period": 22 }` (default), `{ "mode": "spin", "speed": 10 }`, `{ "mode": "still" }` | | `camera` | `{ "elev": 12 }` degrees above the floor | | `click` | `"light"`: a click switches every `light` material (and `glow`) on and off; it starts on | | `pool` | `{ "at": [x, 0, z], "r": 0.2 }`: the light it throws on the floor while on | | `materials` | named materials for the parts | | `motion` | moving groups (joints), below | | `colors` | colourways: `[{ "id": "blue", "name": "Deep blue", "accent": "#2c4f7c" }]` (the accent parts take it; `materials` swaps materials too, at a render each) | | `views` | close-ups and own views: `{ "detail-saddle": { "part": ["saddle*", "seat post"], "angle": -42, "elev": 16, "margin": 1.3, "cover": 2 } }` (a name ending in `*` takes every part it begins; `cover` the widest frame the shot fills, 1 for the margin alone: a close-up render of 2-3 MP takes a CPU 2-9 minutes) | | `scenes` | the product loaded or in use, below | | `supports` | the views the product draws well, `["three-quarter", "side", "front", "detail-saddle"]`: only these are offered (`product.views`), made (`make.variants` outside it fails `--check`) and mounted; list a view only after looking at its still (a bike from above reads as lying on its side, so the city bike omits `top`). Keep `three-quarter` (the default view) | | `make` | `{ "variants": ["three-quarter", "side", "detail-saddle", "three-quarter+loaded"], "grounds": ["light", "dark"], "px": 1100 }`: what make-posters makes | | `parts` | the parts, below (keep it under about 90) | ### Parts Every part takes `mat` (a material name or an inline material), `blend` (a fillet in units where it meets the parts listed before it: welded tubes, a cast body), `in` (a motion group) and `name` (for you). It is placed by `from` + `to` (a linear part runs between them; `up` turns its section), or by `at` plus `axis` (`"x"`, `"y"`, `"z"` or a vector) and/or `rot` ([x, y, z] degrees). | type | sizes | use | |---|---|---| | `tube` | `r`, `r2` (taper), `cap` `flat`/`round`, `round`, `seams` | frame tubes, posts, rods, handles, a tapered robot link | | `beam` | `w`, `d` (section), `round`, `seams` | flat bars, cranks, rails | | `box` | `size` [x, y, z], `round`, `seams` | housings, bodies, pedals, a gripper | | `panel` | `size` (thin), rounder | plates, lids, a screen's back | | `cylinder` / `disc` | `r`, `h`, `round`, `seams` | bases, hubs, motor housings, caps | | `sphere`, `ellipsoid` | `r` / `size` | a bulb, a bell, a knob | | `torus` | `R`, `r` | rings, a chainring, a status light | | `joint` | `r`, `w`, `capMat` | a hinge: knuckle about `axis` (default z) with caps on both faces | | `wheel` | `r`, `tyre` [width, height], `rim` [depth, width], `hub` [r, length], `spokes`, `spokeR`, `style` `spoked`/`disc`/`solid`, `wall` (sidewall colour), `rimMat`, `hubMat`, `spin` (deg/s) | bicycles, strollers, carts, casters; axle along `axis` (default z) | | `shade` | `from` (closed end) `to` (open end), `r1`, `r2`, `t`, `bulge` 0..1, `innerMat` | lamp shades, bells, horns, a speaker cone | | `seat` | `size` [length, height, width], `style` `saddle`/`cushion` | saddles, seats, cushions (local x forward) | | `basket` | `size`, `style` `wire`/`slats`/`solid`, `pitch`, `wire`, `rimMat` | baskets, crates, bins, trays (open top) | | `arc` | `R`, `a0`, `a1` (degrees), `r` or `size` [radial, axial] | mudguards, handles, bent frames, hoops | | `spring` | `from`, `to`, `R`, `r`, `turns` | springs, coiled cords | | `path` | `points` [[x,y,z]...], `r`, `smooth` (on with 3+ points) | handlebars, cables, bent tubes | `seams`: panel lines cut round the part at heights along its length (-1..1 of its half length): the seams of a robot's shell, a base's groove. `seamWidth`, `seamDepth` in units. ### Materials A name from `materials`, a built-in name, or `{ "kind": ..., "color": "#hex" | "accent", "finish": "gloss" | "satin" | "matte" }`. | kind | | built-in names | |---|---|---| | `paint` | enamel or powder coat; `color: "accent"` takes the page's accent | `accent`, `paint`, `white`, `black`, `graphite` | | `metal` | brushed alloy | `alloy`, `aluminium` | | `chrome` | polished | `chrome` | | `steel` | dark stainless (spokes, wire) | `steel` | | `rubber` | tyres, pads, grips | `rubber` | | `plastic` | satin plastic | `plastic` | | `wood` | oiled wood with rings; `grain` x/y/z, `scale` | `wood`, `oak`, `walnut` | | `fabric` | a fine weave; `weave` | `fabric` | | `leather` | | `leather` | | `light` | gives light; with `click: "light"` it switches | `light` | Any material takes `glow` (0..1): a lit inner face (a shade's inside when the lamp is on). ### Motion ```json "motion": [ { "id": "yaw", "pivot": [0, 0.14, 0], "axis": "y", "amp": 26, "period": 13 }, { "id": "shoulder", "parent": "yaw", "pivot": [0, 0.32, 0], "axis": "z", "amp": 9, "period": 11, "phase": 0.2 } ] ``` A group turns its parts (`"in": "shoulder"`) about `pivot` and `axis` by `rest` + `amp` x a sine of `period` seconds, after its parent. Pivots are given at rest, in the spec's units. Up to four groups. The joints move only while the product turns: a still, a phone and reduced motion show the rest pose. ### Scenes and props: the product loaded or in use ```json "scenes": { "loaded": { "label": "A city bicycle with a child seat on the rack, a crate of fruit and a pannier", "hide": ["basket"], "props": [ { "prop": "child-seat", "at": [-0.578, 0.796, 0] }, { "prop": "crate", "at": [0.6, 0.76, 0], "size": [0.3, 0.2, 0.32], "contents": "fruit" }, { "prop": "bag", "at": [-0.62, 0.42, 0.152], "hooks": true } ] }, "desk": { "lit": { "at": [0.53, 0.11], "r": 0.19, "k": 3.6 }, "pool": null, "props": [ { "prop": "desk", "at": [0.2, -0.032, 0.02] }, { "prop": "book", "at": [0.3, 0, -0.15], "count": 2 } ] } } ``` A scene adds props (and plain `parts`), hides parts by name, and may change `label`, `pool`, `click` and `materials`. `lit` throws a lamp's warm pool of light on the props' upward faces. Props are made of ordinary parts at the size of the real thing, standing on y = 0 and facing x, in metres (`scale` converts: 1000 for a spec in millimetres); each takes `at`, `yaw`, `scale`, `size`, `color`, `mats` { role: material }, `in` (a motion group: a parcel held in a gripper) and `name`. | prop | what | options | |---|---|---| | `child-seat` | a rack seat: high back, wings, cushion, shoulder and lap belts to a red buckle, footrests | `color`; roles shell, pad, belt, buckle | | `bench` | a padded bench for 1-3 children or passengers in a row (a cargo box): two belts and a buckle a seat | `seats`, `width`, `color`; roles frame, pad, belt, buckle | | `crate` | a slatted wooden crate, open on top | `size`, `contents` fruit / bottles / loaves / parcels / none | | `bag` | a pannier (flap, straps, handle, `hooks` for a rack) or `style: "tote"` | `size`, `color` | | `parcel` | a cardboard box with tape and a label | `size`, `color` | | `tray` | a low open bin with parcels standing in it | `size`, `parcels` 0-4 | | `desk` | a tabletop | `size`, `color` | | `book` | 1-3 stacked books | `count`, `colors` | | `mug` | a mug of coffee | `r`, `h`, `color` | | `sheet` | a sheet of paper | `size` | Keep a scene under about 110 parts. Its props must read at the size the page shows them (belts, buckles, a crate's slats, a bag's flap), and a scene goes where the copy promises it. ## Behaviour and limits - **It always shows a picture**: the view's still (no WebGL); without one, the poster at once and the render over it, the poster staying when WebGL fails. Under `prefers-reduced-motion`, and on a phone (max-width 700px or a coarse pointer), one still frame, drawn sharp, and the context freed. A turning product has a pause button in its frame's bottom-right corner. - **At most one live context** for a product: only the first product render mounted turns (when the page asks for the turn, or no still was made); a second holds still. The page's cap of 4 contexts (`window.__tpGl`) counts it. - **Cost**: every part is evaluated per ray step, skipped when its bounding sphere is further than the nearest part so far. About 20 parts renders like a print object; 60-70 (a bicycle with its spokes) is fine on a laptop GPU and slow on a CPU renderer (posters: about 90 s). Keep under 90. - **What it cannot do**: text or logos on the product, transparent glass, cloth that drapes, a freeform organic shell (a shoe, a face, a car body), anything thinner than about a texel (it is thickened). For those: the client's photographs or renders, never this. - **Never** a product of another kind, never on a place page, never a caption under it. The three specs in `specs/` (a city bicycle, a desk lamp, a robot arm) are worked examples, each with its views, a scene and colourways (run `make-posters.mjs` on a spec to make its stills; until then each frame renders itself once): `views.html` shows them at anchor scale with colour switches (`?only=bike|lamp|arm`, `?mode=still|live`); `demo.html` the turntable (`?turn=0`, `?fallback=1`).

# Backgrounds

Better grounds come from fewer, better colours (house rule 6: "nicer backgrounds"), and on tech
from a small catalogue of grounds drawn in CSS. Every kind uses the three ground tokens; only tech
adds CSS grounds.

## The three tokens (every kind)

Section and panel grounds use `--g-main`, `--g-alt` and `--g-dark` only (system.css: the base,
`.ground-surface`, `.ground-inverse`): one to three colours down the page, footer included, in the
same order at 390. Photograph layers and the tech grounds below do not count among them.

- **`--g-main`:** white, or a tint of lightness 0.80 to 0.97 with low saturation (channel spread
  0.12 or less), taken from the client: a place's walls, paper or shopfront (the palette
  `start.mjs deal --page place --trade <trade>` deals for its trade, never one fixed off-white for
  every place; white for a shop that sells mostly online), a product's photo backdrop, warm
  greys for a service, blue-leaning or cool grey for software. It covers 55% of the page's height or
  more (60% on software and product). Never pure-white panels on a cream page.
- **`--g-alt`:** the same hue (within 20 degrees), 0.06 to 0.15 darker, never under 0.70
  (`#ffffff` to `#f2f2ef`, `#f7f3ec` to `#ede6da`). Panels, tiles, cards and at most one full band.
- **`--g-dark`:** lightness 0.05 or less: near-black (`#111` to `#1a1a1a`) or the deepest shade of
  the brand hue, never charcoal, never violet. One dark body section at most (one screen tall), at
  the page's middle or later, never right under the hero; the footer may be dark. A dark page (main
  ground 0.02 or darker) and a dark hero are for tech only.
- **The brand band** (`.ground-brand`, product and place): one section in the brand's own colour
  (from the product or the shopfront) may replace the dark band, once, in the second half. On a
  place its lightness is 0.03 to 0.60 and its saturation 0.25 or more, never a neutral near-black;
  every word on it (heading, text, label, link) takes the colour that passes 7:1, the one number: darken the brand colour until it does (`check.mjs` and `consistency.mjs` ask 7:1 for text people read and 4.5:1 for labels, so 7:1 clears both); the primary button is inverted. Otherwise
  saturated colour lives in the accent and the pictures; one mid-tone section at most, never as the
  main ground.
- Grounds change in big blocks at the section edge: never on `.wrap` or a wrapper, no border-top or
  rule between sections, no band inside a section (a box of 80% of its width or more with its own
  ground holding the heading), no inset coloured box standing in for a ground. A frame holding a
  visual is fine.

## Other kinds stay flat

Product, service and place (site-kind other): every ground and panel is a flat CSS colour and
photographs are shown as they are. No gradient (a hard-stop two-tone included), grain, paper,
halo, texture, pattern, glass, contour, canvas, `backdrop-filter`, gradient mask, or shadow or tint
on the interface. Never run `pick.mjs` for them: its `index.json` still lists grounds for product,
service and place, and those are not used. A product page with site-kind tech is dealt as tech.

## Tech: the CSS grounds

Sixteen grounds drawn in CSS (no WebGL) in `assets/backgrounds`. Link `backgrounds.css` after
`system.css` and `cards.css`; load `backgrounds.js` plain at the end of `<head>`. One class on a
section or the hero's wrapper (`<section class="section bg-halo">`); `stage` only as `<div
class="bg-stage">` around one visual card; `paper` on `<body>` and `topglow` around the nav and hero
set no tokens, the thirteen section grounds set the page tokens so cards and buttons work unchanged.
Ink keeps 7:1 and muted 4.5:1 on every palette (`check.mjs` measures it). `index.json` holds each
ground's mood, roles, pairs, avoids and sections.

- **Soft:** `mist` colour wash; `halo` light behind a heading; `ruled` fine grid on the container's
  edges, clear behind the heading; `dots` dots in the margins; `arcs` rings rising, for the close;
  `liquid` a slow mesh of colour ellipses, the only ground that moves.
- **Hard:** `grain` tint with film grain; `dusk` one tone melting into the page; `band` the lit
  ground's second tone; `field` a grainy gradient (Figma's sand tile); `photo` a photograph layer;
  `horizon` a dark band with a lit rim; `deep` near-black with a cool pool (x.ai's).
- **Deal:**

  ```bash
  node <skill>/assets/backgrounds/pick.mjs --type software --sections <the plan's ids> --mode light|dark --history .taste-skill/bg-history.json
  ```

  Hardware runs it as `--type product --kind tech`; with an effect or scene already dealt, add
  `--effect`, and leave the section that holds it (an effect hero, the `[data-visual]` section, the
  scene's section) out of `--sections`: it brings its own ground.

  Mark a section the rhythm already makes a band: `id:dark`, `id:band` (lit ground), `id:surface`.
  Build what it prints, then hold the rules: at most two dealt grounds a page beyond the tokens, each
  once, never on a card, never two strong ones as neighbours, one loud one at most, never two that
  list each other in `avoids`.
- **The effect rule:** a ground with grain, dither or texture (`grain`, `field`, `stage`, `deep`) or
  motion (`liquid`) is the page's one effect (`effects-usage.md`); with another effect dealt, deal
  again without them. `liquid` runs on a clock from load with a pause disc and holds still under
  reduced motion.
- **The lit ground** (`<html data-ground="sand|sky|sage|painting">`) is tech only: behind UI, in a
  closing band, in `footer-statement`; it is the tone of `band` and `field`.
- **Words on `photo`** sit on its calm, dark part (`--g-photo-pos`, `--g-photo-pos-m` for the
  subject); only in the hero and one closing band (`system.md`).
- **Tune:** `--g-hue` tint, `--g-k` strength, `--tone` second tone, `--halo-x`/`--halo-y`,
  `--stage-w`. Tints lean to the accent, never violet.
- A ground never changes a section's height (`layout-v4.md`); a soft one fades over 120px, a hard
  one keeps its colour on the whole box; a panel takes `bg-inset` on the `.wrap` lines.

## Tech: code-drawn grounds, how they look

Calm and specific as a studio photograph: one light, one palette, grain you notice only up close.
Colours from the tokens (`--ground`, `--ground-2`, `--ink`, `--tone`, `--tone-hi` = L +0.12,
`--tone-lo` = L -0.18), mixed in OKLCH, ground chroma under 0.12. A gradient is built light first:
a radial with four to six stops in one hue, then grain (4 to 10%); every dark gradient gets a static
dither; never a two-stop linear gradient as decoration (linear only as an edge fade inside a
visual); a two-tone seam is a hard stop. Grain only inside the one effect: one tile made at load,
never animated, never over UI, text or photographs. Recipes, all still:

- **Lit studio sweep:** behind a cut-out or a UI window: an elliptical radial (50-60% x 40-50%,
  centre 35-42% down), a faint floor bounce, grain 4-6%, a soft contact shadow.
- **Corner glow:** a dark footer, closing band or pricing card: a radial near one corner, radius
  110-130%, five eased stops so no ring shows.
- **Painterly field:** under a UI window or a closing band: four to six large ellipses in the tones,
  blurred 60-120px, drawn 10% oversize and cropped, grain.
- **Spotlight floor:** a hardware stage or a dark hero on a dark page: a light pool 70% wide, a
  blurred shadow running away from the object, side vignettes.
- **Product-colour wash:** a hardware card or model switch: a radial from below in the product's
  tint; it cross-fades on a click, never on scroll.
- **Woven tile and ordered dither:** one texture a page at most: a band, the footer, a technical
  panel.
- **Grid marks** (dots or plus signs at column crossings, 12-18% ink) only on one dark technical
  band, a data panel or the footer, never over text. A hairline ledger (header cells, a line-up,
  footer frame) is 1px repeated sibling rules at 12-15% ink, never between sections.

# Cards How a feature card is built so it looks like x.ai's and Figma's, not a template. Measured from the reference recording (x.ai Grok Bot 2x2, Figma's tile wall) and a study of 41 company sites. Showcase: `assets/ui/cards.html` (nine layouts: 2x2, bento, split, stat, integrations, testimonial, pricing, tall cards, developer tools; light and dark). Every fragment on its own: `assets/ui/index.html`. Styles: `assets/ui/cards.css` (card, panel, placements) and `assets/ui/base.css` (fragments). Motion: `assets/ui/ui.js`. Objects instead of photographs: `assets/ui/_lab/object-card.html`. ## Why theirs look expensive 1. The card is barely there: one step off the page, a hairline, generous padding. The colour is inside the panel. 2. The panel holds a real, lit picture (a painted landscape, a grain field, a mesh, satin), never a flat two-stop gradient and never a pattern of lines or dots. On a dark page it is the brightest thing in the card: x.ai puts a daylight painting behind its dark UI. 3. The UI on it is a real product at true size, cut by the panel's edge: a glimpse of something bigger, not a toy floating in the middle. 4. One thing moves per card group, inside a panel (tech pages). The card never moves by itself; a card with a link lifts 2px on hover (`motion.md`). 5. Everything lines up: panel edge with text edge, radii nested, titles level across a row. ## The card - Fill `--card`, one clear step off the page (light: white on `#f3f3f1`; dark: `#151517` on `#070708`, as x.ai's dark cards read against their page), or no border at all when the photograph or flat fill is the card. - Border 1px, ink at 8 to 14%; inner top highlight 1px (white 5-7%, dark only). No blurred shadow at rest (a hard zero-blur offset is allowed as the rest style); a card with a link may show a soft shadow on hover only (`motion.md`). A card with a link lifts 2px on hover; a card without one carries `.m-nolift`. Never tilted, never a carousel: rows show whole cards; press quotes stack. - Rows on the grid: two-up 6+6, three-up 4+4+4, four-up 3+3+3+3, the first card on the left line, the last on the right, one height per row, every row full (`layout-v4.md` section 4). Mark every frame that holds a visual or UI with `.frame` or `[data-visual]` so it never counts as a band. - Radius `--r-lg` (20 on `soft`; 18 on a phone). Padding 32 from 1024px, 28 below, 24 on a phone: never under 24, and the text always inside it. A filled split panel pads 48. - Title one line at the card-title token (20/18), weight 500. 8px, then at most two lines at 16/24 in the ink (`--c-text`, 84% ink: never small grey text), at most 46ch. All running text in a card is 16/24 in that ink: points, the line under a stat, plan lines and lists, a quote's name and role, a result's bar labels. Muted small text is for labels only (a price's "/ month", a section tag). `.card--row` holds the lines at 2 from 1024px so titles and panels line up across a row. - 32px from the last line to the panel. One `--p-h` per card group (page CSS), and a phone value beside it when the group's tiles stack into a two-screen section (`@media (max-width: 639px) { #features .panel { --p-h: 180px } }` holds four tiles of two lines each in two phone screens). ## Two levels, never three A card holds a picture, and the picture holds the product. That is all: - **card > panel (a lit picture) > fragment.** The panel must read as a picture, not as a box: a soft field with no border lines, grid, ruling or dots of its own, so the fragment sits *on a picture*, not in a frame in a frame. - Never card > patterned panel > white UI card (in testing, "card, grid-paper panel, white UI card" read as three nested boxes). Never a fragment that is itself a card holding cards of text. - Never a card inside a card for text, never glass. ## The panel - Default (x.ai): side edges on the text column, runs off the card's bottom edge, top radius 12, the lower 60-65% of the card (`--p-h` 264-340px). - `.panel--inset`: even 8px margin; radius = card radius - margin (20 - 8 = 12), never under 6, so the corners read as one family. Every panel in a row has one ratio (4:3 or 16:10) and one inset. A smaller UI card on a panel is solid (never frosted), 40 to 60% of the panel's width, offset so the panel's bottom or right edge cuts it. - `.panel--flush`: runs to the card's side and bottom edges (Figma's image band). - `.panel--top`: on top with an 8px margin, the card's lines below (tall cards). - `.panel--device`: a status row on the card itself (app, muted context, a quiet status with a still dot), then the ground as its screen, radius 12, running off the bottom: x.ai's "Computer" card. The row is not a frame of its own (a filled device frame made a fourth box). - A 1px inner edge (`::after`) sits over the ground and over any fragment it cuts. - The vignette (`::before`: `--vx`, `--vy`, `--calm-k`) calms the ground where the fragment sits. On a lit ground set `--calm-k: 0%` and use the effect's own `calm` params. ## The fragment on it - **The product's own subject**: the fragment shows what this product works on, as its users see it. A code-review tool shows a real diff, red and green, with the comment and its Accept or Apply action (`diff-review`); an invoicing app an invoice; a booking app its calendar; a CI product its pipeline (`pipeline-board`, `terminal-run`). Never a generic dashboard, chat or stat card standing in for it; when no fragment shows the subject, build it from the client's screens. Cards show parts; the product is shown whole once, big, in an `app-frame` (`sections-library.md`: `window` as the list beside the open item, one window across the `.wrap`). A software page whose product appears only as small fragments centred on coloured panels reads as fragments, not as the product (in testing: about 3.5 points under Linear). A gaming page takes no fragment at all: it shows the game (`sections.md`, Gaming). Its feature cards are open cards for what you do in it, one verb each (sail, salvage, rebuild), each holding an in-engine shot, else the still render of the object that verb uses (`data-product-place="card"`). - The product's real UI as live HTML at true size, complete and legible, never a flat picture: 13px text, 12px meta, never under 11px; weights 400 and 500. Real data (names, amounts, order numbers, times) and real app marks (`icons.md`). Each fragment keeps its minimum width (chat 140, checklist 160, slider 215, toggles 230, search 240, terminal-run 280, calendar 280, stat 285, cursor 290, files 300, diff-review 280, pipeline-board 280, notify 340, code 365, doc 400, window 456). A phone mock or UI card runs past its panel only where the panel clips it, never past `.wrap`. - Surface white on light, `#1c1d20` on dark (one step lighter than the `#151517` card; `--frag` sets it); 1px border at 12%; radius 12; the layered shadow lives only inside the panel. - The primary button is the ink; switches that are on are ink; the product's own mark (`.ui-agent`) is ink. **The accent appears once per fragment**: the row being worked on, the marked date, the marked line's bar, the last bar, the slider being dragged. A range, keywords, numbers, today's dot and status chips are ink tints. Never a row of green dots. - **Real icons in their own colours** (house rule: "more colour, more official"): a mark on a tile (`.ui-logo`, `.ui-file__icon`, `.ui-field__tile`) sits on a light tile on every surface, in its brand colours: a colour file from `assets/icons` (`icons.mjs fetch` or `scan`, `references/icons.md`) as ``. The kit's sample marks are local files in `assets/ui/icons` (``): after pasting, write each as the client's tool, ``, and `icons.mjs scan --colour` fetches it; no page calls a CDN for an icon. One treatment per set: never colour marks beside ink marks. A small mark inline beside text (a breadcrumb, a source chip) stays in the ink. Glyph marks only; a wordmark (Zoom's) is illegible at tile size. - Placement (`.stage` holds them, absolute in the panel; each `meta.json` has its own `place`): - `.at-corner`: 28-40px from the top-left, cut by the right and bottom (19 of 41 sites). - `.at-rise`: starts 24-56px down and leaves through the bottom (chat, voice, a calendar). - `.at-right`: anchored top-right; it narrows on a small panel rather than cut its text. - A short stack (notify) sits low: `--ay` and `--ay-sm` `calc(100% - 180px)`, its last row cut. - `.at-over`: a second fragment over the first one's lower-right edge. The `cursor` dialog only ever sits here, over a window: never alone on a ground, never centred. - `.at-center`: only a small control (at most about 250 x 130) on a focal tile: the compact slider driving its ground (Figma's Texture tile). Never a window or a dialog. It never runs past the panel (cards.css caps it at the panel less 24px a side, 16px on a phone). - `.fit` + `--fit-max: `: keeps its width on a wide panel, centred between the insets (even ground at both sides), and narrows on a small one, so 1024 never shows a 1-23px sliver or cut. `window` lays itself out for the width it gets (rows stack under 540px, the sidebar goes under 420px), so it may sit in a `.fit`. - `.wide` + `--w`: a fluid grid (files) set wider than the panel, so it is cut by the right edge like a window; it always runs 64px or more past it. - `.to-edge`: the wrapper reaches 72px past the bottom, whatever the panel's height; `chat`, `doc`, `stat` (`fill`) and `voice` grow into it, so they are always cut, never a few px short. - Developer tools (tech and software pages only; all three lay themselves out for the width they get, so none is ever sliced): - `diff-review` (a code review on a diff): `.at-corner.fit` (or `.at-rise.fit` in a wide panel) with `--fit-max: 480px` (up to 760px wide), 32-40px in, cut by the bottom with `.stage--fade-b`: the reviewed line, its suggestion, the comment and the Apply button stay in the top 250px, and the diff runs two context lines further, so a 352px panel at 36px down cuts it by 32px or more at every width (never leave less than 24px of it past the edge). Never cut it by the right edge. Under 440px it keeps one gutter and drops the function name from the hunk header; on a phone give its panel 340px or more. The file's real mark (TypeScript) sits on a light tile in its header. The accent is the short bar beside the comment's text, set in from the comment's edge. - `terminal-run` (a test run in a terminal): `.at-rise.fit` with `--fit-max: 440px`, 32-40px in and 32-40px down, always whole with 24px or more of ground under it (a 352px panel at 40px down). Never cut or faded: the status line with its green check sits one row above the bottom. In a wide panel or a split card `--fit-max` goes up to 560px (the path column stops at 28 characters). The counts go under 380px; the branch and the repo's parent folder under 300px. The status check is the one green and the strongest mark; the meter's thin bar is the one accent; the per-file ticks stay ink. - `pipeline-board` (a CI run on a rail of steps) sits whole: `.at-rise.fit` with `--fit-max: 420px`, 32-40px down, 24px or more of ground under it and no fade, since the running step reaches the last row. In a large panel or a split card it goes `.at-corner.fit` at its full width (680px or more), where it becomes a row of nodes with a log about 300px tall, and the bottom-right corner stays clear for the pause button. Waiting steps say "Queued" in the markup, so no node is an empty box. Each step names the real mark of its tool (Git, npm, Node.js, Docker, Kubernetes) on a light tile, one treatment for all five. The cycle starts and ends on the markup as written, so write the picture to rest on (the run part done). - Vary the placements across a group: a 2x2 shows at least three (rise, corner or device, a low stack, right). Never one card layout four times. ## Edges and fades - Every edge keeps 24px of ground or is cut by 24px or more (16px a side on a phone, by design). A cut never slices text: `.stage--fade-b`, `--fade-r`, `--fade-br` dissolve the last `--fade-h` (64px; 40px on a short panel such as the tall cards) into the ground. - **A fade never crops the point.** It only covers context: the row below the one that changes, a chat's input, a page's later paragraphs, a list's last rows. The thing the card is about (the row being worked on, the connecting app, the number, the button, the orb and its transcript line) sits above `100% - --fade-h`. Put the moving row near the top (the integrations target third, not last), or lower the fragment's start, or shorten the fade. - A fade only where an edge cuts: a fragment that keeps 24px of ground on a side has no fade on that side (`--fade-br` on a window that ends inside the panel fades it for nothing). - Measure at 1440, 1024, 768 and 390; on a phone cards.css places the fragment 16px in on both sides, cut only at the bottom. ## Grounds Shader grounds in panels are for tech pages (software and hardware; a gaming page has no feature cards of UI), one card group a page, still, from the family of the page's one effect (`effects-usage.md`). On a product or service page a panel holds the client's photograph (``, zooming 1.02 to 1.03 inside it when the card links), real icons or a still diagram on a flat `--g-alt` or `--g-main` panel; a place has no feature cards. Other tech card groups take a flat panel, the lit ground plain, a photograph or a diagram. - One ground id for the card group, a new `data-fx-seed` per panel, never the id of the hero's effect (one effect in hero, cards and close reads as a stock motif). - **Behind a fragment, a soft field**: `painterly-landscape`, `grain-gradient`, `gradient-mesh`, `silk-folds` (and other mesh, grain and material families). Never a pattern that fights the UI: no `grid-pulse`, `ruled-grounds`, `contour-lines`, `dot-terrain`, `ridgeline`, `halftone-screen` or `bayer-dither` behind a window, list or card. Those are pictures on their own: a panel with no fragment, an object's print, or the data cut out of the UI (below). - Lit behind UI, on both themes: give each panel that holds UI a light `data-fx-palette` of its own, the same in light and dark. On the dark page it is clearly lighter than the card (3:1 or more), so page, card, panel and UI are never four near-black layers; on the light page it is a clear step darker than the white UI. The palettes in the showcase: - painting: `{"bg":"#a3b0b6","accent":"#c49a6c"}` with params `"blur":1,"brush":0.35,"slope":0, "hillY":0.3,"horizon":0.62` (a level mist over warm sand, fully soft). Never a blue sky over a green hill with a diagonal crest: it reads as a stock desktop wallpaper, not a crafted ground. At most one painted panel in a card group (one per page is better); the others take the sand, sky or sage palette on grain, mesh or silk. - sand: `{"bg":"#d9ccb7","surface":"#e9e0d2","ink":"#2a2622","accent":"#a8794a"}` - sky: `{"bg":"#c6d3df","surface":"#d6e0e9","ink":"#25303a","accent":"#3f6a92"}` (silk-folds takes a softer accent, `#7f9fbd`, with `"tone":1`) - sage: `{"bg":"#cdd6c6","surface":"#dce3d6","ink":"#262d24","accent":"#6c8e63"}` - A calm hue of its own keeps the page's accent rare. Never violet or lavender. - Hold every ground still in a card: `speed` 0 or `drift` 0, and `grainMotion` 0 on grain-gradient (its film grain moves otherwise). Where the bottom fade shows the ground, calm it there (`calmY` near 1) so the fade meets a quiet field, not a bright highlight. - A ground shows something behind something. A strip of effect under a stat or a line of text, holding nothing, is decoration: leave the card plain (Figma's "64%" is a number and one line). ## Light on a laptop GPU Every page must run on an integrated laptop GPU (2 GB shared), so: - system.js mounts card grounds through `ui.grounds(document, fx)` (a page without system.js calls it itself, never `fx.mountAll`): each still ground is drawn once as it nears the screen, at up to 2 device pixels (sharp on a 1.25-2x laptop), kept as a plain picture, and its WebGL context freed, one at a time, the panel on screen first (a scroll past a group never makes the one in view wait). A ground a fragment drives (the slider) carries `data-fx-live`: it is live near the screen only, at 1 device pixel, and draws only when it changes; under reduced motion it is baked like the rest. - Live contexts: the page's one effect is the moving hero ground (system.js keeps it live) or one of these: the driven ground, the voice orb (dark surfaces only; on light it is CSS), a hover light (the featured plan's lap), an object (`effects-usage.md`). Never two of them on a page. `ui.grounds` bakes the card grounds one at a time (one context while baking, none after: `effects-creative.md`, Cost) and caps the `fx` library at 3 live contexts; the page's cap of 4 (`perf.md`) counts everything live at once, the effect, a scene and a moment's canvas included. It leaves `fx.config.maxDpr` alone. - An object or any raymarched canvas mounts when its panel nears the screen and is destroyed when it leaves (`_lab/object-card.html`); one per card group; never two objects and a moving ground in one view. It renders at most 1 CSS px per pixel (0.75 when large), about 1.5 megapixels, and stops off screen and in a hidden tab. ## Motion Card loops are for tech pages; every number (cycle, restart, pause disc, life signs) is in `motion.md`. The same rule as system.js, in one line: **put `data-ui-loop` on the group's one loop; every other fragment holds its finished picture.** - With system.js nothing else is needed: it marks every other fragment `data-ui-still` before it loads, and on a phone (under 640px) every fragment but `voice`. - Without system.js (`cards.html`), `ui.loadAll` / `ui.startAll` do the same as soon as the page holds any `data-ui-loop`. A page with none (the kit's `index.html`) lets every fragment loop. - The group's loop is the one whose motion shows the point (the slider that drives the ground, the chat answering). `voice` always runs (held, it loses its orb), so it is its group's loop. `data-ui-still` holds a fragment by hand; `data-ui-cycles="2"` plays two cycles when first seen, then rests on the finished picture, with no button. - Below the hero, two loops are never on one screen: a group next to a looping one holds still. - ui.js puts a pause button on every loop when it starts to move: a solid 32px disc in the page colours. In a `.card` it sits beside the card's title, at the right of the text column (the title keeps 44px clear for it), so it never covers a cropped panel's UI, which runs into every corner. In `[data-ui-pause-host]`, or a `.panel`/`.frame` outside a card, it sits 12px in from the bottom-right corner (keep that corner clear); a fragment with no panel gets it under its bottom-right corner, in 44px kept free. A place that already holds a `.loop-pause` gets no second one. Keyboard focus in a card plays a held fragment's cycle once; only a pointer resting on the card repeats it (a held fragment has no button). - Anything else that moves on its own for more than 5 s (an object, a moving ground) gets the same button: `ui.pausable(panel, ctrl)`, where `ctrl` has `pause()` and `resume()`. - Loops start on the finished picture and never show an empty window or greyed text: the chat writes only its answer's last sentence again, and the voice its transcript line, each in under 0.8 s with no word below 72% ink (4.5:1 on white), then hold the finished text for the rest of the cycle. The files status line shows only the page's words (`data-reading="Reading {n} of {total}"` on the root, in the page's language; without it only the line's number counts). A tile the panel cuts hides its name, never half a word. They stop off screen and hold still under reduced motion (no buttons then). Nothing moves because the page scrolled. - **Cadence and hover** (house rule 5): one cycle of 2.5 to 4 s that repeats and restarts when the pointer or focus enters the card; every number is in `motion.md`, Loops inside a card's visual. A card whose fragments are all held plays its top fragment while the pointer stays. The card itself never moves by itself. - **From the page**: `ui.restart(el)` restarts every fragment in `el` (a tab or panel shown again); a held one plays once. Every fragment root fires a bubbling `ui-cycle` event as each cycle starts, for a page that keeps a second piece in step. - **The page's words, never the kit's**: a fragment's script shows only text from the markup. Its finished picture is the markup as written (the doc's note, the slider's value, the stat's number, the voice transcript and timer); its other states are written beside the text they change (`data-done`, `data-busy`, `data-note`, `data-msg`, `data-work`) or passed as opts. A count keeps its words and only its figure follows ("4 of 5 on" reads "3 of 5 on"). ## Effects that are not backgrounds - **The control drives the ground**: `slider` with `{"drive":{"param":"grain"}}` changes the panel effect as the thumb moves. Make it the group's loop. `{"compact":true}` keeps the name and the one slider, small enough for `.at-center` on a focal tile. - **Data cut out of the UI**: `stat` with `{"window":true}` cuts its bars out, so the ground shows through them. - **A number filled with an effect**: `.knock`, a still canvas under white text with `mix-blend-mode: darken` on dark (black text, `lighten`, on light); the card fill must be exactly `--card`. - **A live object in the UI**: on a dark surface `voice` mounts `orb-sphere` as the call's orb, a pale nebula with specks of light (x.ai's voice orb); on a light surface it is a pearl drawn in CSS with clouds of the accent and the ink turning slowly inside it and a few specks of light, never a plain white disc. The accent is only the thin ring round it. Never a dark glass ball on a light card. - **A real object, no photograph** (tech only): an object from `assets/objects` is the whole picture of a `.panel--top` on one of the lit palettes above, centred because it is the subject; how to mount, print and pause it is in `effects-objects.md`. It turns, never tilts the card. - **A lit border** on the one featured object: `data-glow="edge-glow"` and `data-glow-params='{"fill":1,"wash":0,"speed":400,...}'` on the featured plan (never `data-fx`). It rests on a quiet accent hairline; on hover or keyboard focus one light runs round the edge (about 4.6 s, mounted for that lap only), then fades. Never on scroll or on view. The hairline is the plan's one accent, so its badge is quiet ink. ## Never - A big fragment dead centre with even ground all round; a dialog alone on a ground. - Three levels of boxes: a card, a patterned panel, a white card on it. - A pattern (grid, ruling, contours, dots) behind a window or a list. - A fade over the point of a fragment; a sliver of 1-23px at any edge. - A dark ground behind dark UI on a dark page. - The accent on every chip, date and keyword; brand colours mixed with ink marks; glossy 3D blobs. - A loop over 5 s with no pause button; a spinner, caret or pulse running on in a still picture. - A card or panel that moves with scroll or lights up when it scrolls into view. - One WebGL context per panel, or a still ground left running its frame loop. - A "sample", "example" or "to follow" note anywhere, even one line in the footer (in testing: "Names and figures on this page are examples" read as an apology), a caption under a visual that explains or apologises, and a placeholder (`[Name]`, `Example Street 1`, a `.example` address, lorem ipsum). Licence credits go in one footer line. - Small grey card text (15px muted): card text is 16px in the ink.

# Copy moves

The move for each part of the page, distilled from a study of professional sites written before
language models (2014 to 2021). Every example here is written for this file, for made-up clients: learn
the move, never the line. The rules of `copy.md` hold throughout: the h1 names the category, every
heading has its noun, buttons are a verb and an object, nothing is invented.

## The hero

Professional heroes are short (2 to 9 words), one clause, never two adjectives stacked. On a tasteskill
page the h1 names the category, so the form is chosen among the ones that do:

| Form | Example | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Category and buyer | "Payroll app for restaurant teams" | software, a service nobody knows yet |
| Category and place | "Bakery on Mill Street, Leith" | every place |
| Category and a true, unexpected promise | "Tax return app that asks eleven questions" | the category is known and the twist is in the brief |
| Category and one striking customer | "Rota planner for the night shift at three hospitals" | the brief names that customer and it may be shown |
| Category and scope | "Card payments for market stalls" | infrastructure, B2B with a real scope |
| Category, place and year | "Guesthouse on the lake shore since 1962" | the brief gives the year |
| A narrow superlative | "The only ferry to the island in winter" | the brief proves it, and the next line says how |
| Name and genre | "Kelpmoor, a co-op sailing game" | a game |

The other forms professionals use (a greeting, a line to the reader's state of mind, a question, an
imperative, an enemy, a twisted idiom, product news) never take the h1. They can take the sub-line, a
section's first line, the close, or the page's one brand line, each with a fact beside it:

- **The reader's state:** "Three hundred emails since Friday? The inbox sorts them by sender before you
  open it."
- **An enemy, a habit or a category:** "Most booking forms ask for your life story. Ours asks for two
  dates."
- **Product news, plain:** "New this spring: the 12-litre model, same price."

**The sub-line:** software and services: how it works and the main benefit, 15 to 30 words, one fact or
one mechanism, never a row of adjectives. A place: the fact with today's hours, 80 characters at most.

## Section headings

- **The name with a claim under it** is the default: a heading that names the part ("Rooms and
  prices") and one line under it that claims ("Six rooms, all with the lake on one side").
- **A verb and the thing** works where the reader does something: "Send invoices from the van", "Plan
  the week's shifts". Never a bare command ("Get started", "Come climb").
- **A plain claim with its noun:** "Pays staff on the same day".
- **A figure from the brief:** "212 routes, reset every Tuesday".
- **Questions only in the FAQ.** A heading is never a question (`copy.md`); the line under the close's
  heading may ask once, plainly, when the register allows it.

## About and story

1. **Start in a moment the brief gives, not a thesis:** the day the oven arrived, the first market
   stall, the season the river flooded the cellar.
2. **Anecdotes, a timeline or questions, never value pillars** ("Our values: quality, community,
   passion" is the weakest about page there is).
3. **Failure and luck belong in the plot** when the brief has them: the first plan that did not work,
   the landlord who said yes.
4. **Founders as people, not titles,** and only the names the brief gives.
5. **Values as behaviours with numbers:** "We pay growers twice the market price"; a rule, not an
   adjective.
6. **End in a modest present tense,** not a vision: "Eleven of us now, and the same oven."
7. **Say how to reach them:** the form, the street, the hours.

A portfolio's about: one line with what the person does (a deflating word welcome), what they make and
for whom, one or two projects with dates, one sentence of belief, availability as a plain date.

## Features and how it works

- **The mechanism in verb-led steps:** "Forward the invoice. The app reads the total and the due date.
  It pays on the day you choose."
- **The outcome first, the feature as its proof:** "Nobody misses a shift change", then how the
  reminder works.
- **A moment, not a use case:** "Your drummer cancels at six; the stand-in gets the set list at
  6:01."
- **Real values in the examples:** times, sizes, amounts, never "customisable".
- **The product doing the work:** UI fragments with the client's own data, names and numbers
  (`cards.md`). On tech the UI carries most of the words (`copy.md`, the tech word budget).
- **Names are copy too:** rooms, plans, blends and models the brief names, used the same way every
  time.
- **Card length varies with the material:** a title (a verb and an object) and one or two sentences;
  a card the brief knows a lot about may run longer than its neighbours.

## Proof

- **Only what the brief gives:** quotes word for word with the name and role or town, figures with
  their source, logos of real customers who may be shown.
- **Let others say the superlatives,** with full attribution.
- **Rough beats polished:** a real quote stays as written, lowercase and all.
- **A rule instead of a claim:** "Every frame is brazed by the person who measured you" proves the
  craft without the word.
- **None is fine.** Craft, luxury and small places often show no testimonials: the photographs and the
  facts carry the page.

## Prices, FAQ, booking: the plain zone

- **The tone drops to facts:** the reader is anxious here.
- **Perks priced and literal:** "Late checkout until 14:00 for 15 euro", "Bike hire 12 euro a day".
- **A risk reversal beside the button, only when true:** "Cancel up to two days before, free".
- **Admit limits in the FAQ:** "Android comes next year; today it is iPhone only."
- **Ask the buyer's real objection and answer it flatly:** "Can I take my data out? Yes: every table
  exports as CSV, any time."

## Buttons and the close

- **A verb and the real object** (`copy.md` rule 4): "Book a room", "Order a cake", "Start a free
  trial".
- **Literal even when the register plays:** the button says what happens next.
- **A low-pressure exit for browsers** where the register fits: "See the rooms first".
- **The close restates the hero's promise with one fact** from the brief, and the main action word for
  word.

## Microcopy: where a voice is most welcome

Write these whenever the page has them; a stock form error under a hand-tuned hero gives the game
away. The form rules of `copy.md` hold (a label says what goes in, an error names the field and what to
type, the sent line names what was sent in the button's words); the register shows in the words around
them:

- **Form error:** "Mondays we are closed: choose a day from Tuesday to Sunday."
- **Sent message:** "Your table request is in. We answer before noon the next day." (the time from the brief)
- **Empty state:** "No notes yet. Your first meeting lands here when it ends."
- **404:** "This page moved. The menu and the hours are one click up."
- **Newsletter confirmation:** "Subscribed. The next letter goes out on the first Sunday of the
  month." (the rhythm from the brief)
- **Field hint:** "Only for this booking." (and only what the brief promises)

## The footer

Facts only: the legal row of `copy.md` (the brand, this year, Privacy, Terms, the credits line), the
street and district, the hours on a place. No sign-off, no pun built on the name.

## Numbers and humour

- **Odd human numbers beat round big ones:** "eleven people came to the first tasting", "45 seconds
  per side", when the brief gives them.
- **Every number sits in a sentence,** beside the claim it proves.
- **Humour points at ourselves, never the customer,** and lives in brackets, asides and microcopy, not
  at the end of every paragraph. None on a serious purchase (money, health) beyond the microcopy.
- **Rhythm on purpose, once:** a run of short sentences that paints a scene, a list that ends on a
  surprise, one long sentence beside a short one.

# Copy registers

The voices to choose from, drawn from how professional sites wrote before language models (2014 to
2021). Choose one per client; borrow a single move from a second. Every sample line is written for this
file, for a made-up client. A register shapes the sub-line, the body, the story and the microcopy; it
never bends the rules of `copy.md` (the h1's category, the headings' nouns, the buttons' verbs).

**None is the default.** Choose by the buyer, the price and the client's real character; when the brief
does not settle it, take the register least like the last page this session wrote.

## 0. The model's default (the one to avoid)

Warm, wry, modest, a little literary, mildly against big companies. Paragraphs end on a deadpan twist;
sincerity comes from honest, calm, quiet, actually; a strip of figures, three polished quotes, a pun in
the footer. Use it only when the client asks for it, and then within the device budget.

## 1. Facts only

- **Sounds like:** "Kessler Partners advises family firms on succession. Founded 1994, nine partners,
  offices in Basel and Freiburg."
- **Moves:** plain declaratives with names, dates and counts; third person or a terse first person;
  exclusivity shown by a rule or a fact, never by an adjective.
- **Fits:** a strong track record, professional services, B2B infrastructure, clubs, consultants.
- **Fails when:** the facts are weak. Then it reads as an empty CV.

## 2. Technical and dry, with proof

- **Sounds like:** "Every pull request gets its own database, seeded from last night's backup. Branch
  in 4 seconds; delete it on merge."
- **Moves:** a label paired with a hard figure; the mechanism in verb-led steps; real commands, UI
  strings and file names on the page; the enemy is a category ("most preview setups"); jargon kept on
  purpose for experts or translated once; the product as the subject of the sentence.
- **Fits:** developer tools, infrastructure, APIs, technical software.
- **Fails when:** it turns into a spec dump with no pain named, or into abstractions ("power and
  alignment").

## 3. The founder's letter

- **Sounds like:** "We ran a print shop for eleven years and lost a day a week to quotes. So we built
  the quoting tool we wanted, and now 300 shops use it."
- **Moves:** first person; a named habit or a category as the enemy; the reader's pain in their own
  words; a refrain used on purpose; an argument carried across the sections, each paragraph within
  `copy.md`'s lengths; a plain human sign-off in the text (never the footer).
- **Fits:** products with a stance, small software companies, anything founder-led and against the way
  things are done.
- **Fails when:** the stance is put on, or the founder has no real argument.

## 4. Self-aware and playful

- **Sounds like:** "Hot sauce from one farm in Kent. Medium is hot. Hot is a mistake you make once."
- **Moves:** a straight face about a small product; the joke in the sub-line or a card, with the fact
  right under it; house words the brief gives; the microcopy in full voice; failures on display. Hype
  words stay out even as a joke: copy-lint FAILs them, ironic or not.
- **Fits:** drinks, snacks, small consumer goods, small studios, playful apps.
- **Fails when:** the jokes are random, aimed at the customer, or put on a serious purchase (money,
  health).

## 5. Literary and formal

- **Sounds like:** "A balm for hands worn by cold water and rope. Citrus, cedar, a little smoke. 75 ml,
  34 euro."
- **Moves:** an exact, slightly raised vocabulary; "clients", not "customers"; sensory notes in tight
  lists; materials and botanicals by name; never an exclamation mark; the price plain on the button.
- **Fits:** skincare, fragrance, design objects, high-end retail.
- **Fails when:** it turns ornate without being exact ("a luxurious ritual of the senses").

## 6. Proper nouns and restraint

- **Sounds like:** "The old customs house above the harbour, built 1871. Eight rooms face the strait;
  the ferry to the island leaves below the terrace at 7:40."
- **Moves:** places, history, buildings and geography do the work; unhurried physical verbs (overlook,
  stroll, reside); no prices in the hero, no quotes; the story in three sentences and a date. The word
  "luxury" never appears.
- **Fits:** luxury hotels, heritage houses, architecture practices, galleries.
- **Fails when:** there is no real place or history in the brief to name.

## 7. Sensory facts, second person, present tense

- **Sounds like:** "You order at the counter beside the roaster. The cardamom buns come out at 8:00
  and again at 11:00."
- **Moves:** what the reader will see, smell, hear or carry, each one a literal fact of the place (the
  oven, the hour, the floor, the weight); craft shown as a repeated step and a constraint; one defining
  absence ("no mirrors in the studio"); odd human numbers. Never a metaphor or a mood paragraph: the
  floor of `copy.md` holds.
- **Fits:** cafes, food, bars, fitness, yoga, spas, anything consumed with the body.
- **Fails when:** every section turns sensory. Prices and booking stay plain.

## 8. Historical scene

- **Sounds like:** "In 1958 the tram stopped outside, and the bakery opened at five for the drivers. It
  still does."
- **Moves:** opens on a dated moment, not on the brand; streets, furniture and people named; old
  photographs as evidence, never captioned on the page (`copy.md`).
- **Fits:** restaurants, family firms, anything with a real lineage in the brief.
- **Fails when:** the history is invented or generic ("rooted in tradition").

## 9. Plain-spoken activist

- **Sounds like:** "Every jacket we sell, we take back. In 2025 that was 3,140 jackets, and 2,200 went
  back on sale."
- **Moves:** a mission in one measurable sentence; the hard subject said plainly; admits its own harm;
  buttons that act on the mission; proof in numbers and reports.
- **Fits:** mission-led consumer brands, non-profits, firms with real impact figures in the brief.
- **Fails when:** the mission is a paragraph of abstract nouns ("inspiring healthier communities").

## 10. Refusal and narrowness

- **Sounds like:** "We repair bicycles. Not e-bikes, not scooters. Bicycles, in two days, at the bench
  you can see from the street."
- **Moves:** positioned by what it will not do; scarcity stated as an honest limit; the makers named
  when the brief names them; a ritual as community.
- **Fits:** makers, small batches, specialists, single-product companies.
- **Fails when:** the refusal is invented to sound focused. (It spends the page's negation run.)

## 11. The product as the hero

- **Sounds like:** "The X2 runs 140 minutes on a charge and climbs a 2 cm sill. It maps the flat on the
  first run."
- **Moves:** almost no "we"; the product is the subject of every sentence; a turn of phrase is followed
  at once by a spec; one moment from life ("crumbs under the sofa at 22:00").
- **Fits:** hardware, physical products, apps with one strong feature.
- **Fails when:** a play on words has no fact under it.

## 12. Hurried and conversational

- **Sounds like:** "Packaging for small food brands, by three people in one studio in Bristol (the one
  who answers the phone also draws the box)."
- **Moves:** talks to one busy person; asides in brackets; self-deprecation; casual section labels that
  still name the thing; permission to leave.
- **Fits:** small studios, freelancers, portfolios, direct-to-consumer brands with a founder.
- **Fails when:** it gets chummy ("We get it.") or the jokes replace the information.

## Matching voice to the trade (starting points only)

| Trade | Try first | Avoid |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cafe, roastery, bakery | 7 sensory, 8 historical, 4 playful | 0 the default |
| Developer tool, infrastructure | 2 technical-dry, 3 founder's letter | 4 playful in the hero |
| Software for small businesses | 3 founder's letter, 11 product as hero | abstract "power and alignment" |
| AI product | 2 technical-dry, 11 product as hero | "magic", "superpowers" |
| Agency, studio | 1 facts only, 12 hurried, 4 playful | stacked category nouns ("digital brand experience company") |
| Portfolio | 12 hurried, 1 facts only | a list of credits with no person in it |
| Luxury hotel | 6 restraint | the word "luxury" |
| Guesthouse, small hotel | 12 hurried, 7 sensory, 6 restraint | "boutique", "curated experiences" |
| Fitness, yoga | 7 sensory, 10 refusal | "the best version of yourself" |
| Architecture | 6 restraint, 1 facts only | "spaces that inspire" |
| Course, teaching | 3 the teacher's letter, 7 sensory for a physical skill | "transform your life" |
| Skincare, beauty | 5 literary, 10 refusal | "clean", "glow" with no ingredient |
| Finance | 1 facts only, 3 founder's letter | jokes about money worries, unsourced savings |
| Hardware, appliances | 11 product as hero, 2 technical-dry | adjectives where the spec should be |
| Game | the game's own world and tone, 12 for the studio | the default register on the store page |
| Drinks, snacks | 4 playful, 9 activist | 0 the default |
| Repair shop, trade | 10 refusal, 1 facts only | "passion", "quality you can trust" |
| Wedding, events, photography | 7 sensory, 12 hurried | "capturing your special day" |

# Copy tells

What makes website copy read as model-written, with the fix for each. Dated November 2026: the tells
move with every model generation, so learn why each one reads as a model and do not just memorise the
list. One tell proves little; clusters and repetition are the signal. `scripts/copy-lint.mjs` counts the
ones that can be counted; its id is in brackets.

Severity: **ban** (one is a tell), **cap** (fine once, a tell when repeated), **context** (counts only
beside other tells).

## Why it happens

A model picks the phrasing that fits the most pages, and tuning smooths it toward safe, positive,
dense prose. The odd true fact gets replaced by a claim that fits any business. So the specific has to
come from the input (the brief, the client's words), never from style rules; and every rule that bans a
habit needs a positive move beside it, or the model reaches for the nearest substitute.

## First generation: the old tells (mostly avoided now; still checked)

- **Ban words** [copy-slop-word]: delve, tapestry, testament to, realm, embark, beacon, multifaceted,
  paradigm, myriad, plethora, meticulous, intricate, interplay, garner, boasts (for "has"); elevate,
  unlock, unleash, empower, harness, supercharge, turbocharge, seamless, effortless, cutting-edge,
  revolutionary, transformative, holistic, next-level, next-generation, world-class, best-in-class,
  game-changer, game-changing, state-of-the-art, bespoke, synergy, leverage, reimagine, powerful,
  robust, nestled, unparalleled, unrivalled. Each stands in for a fact: "seamless" for the setup steps,
  "robust" for the failure case, "powerful" for the figure. A word that is literal for the trade stays:
  a climbing harness, bespoke tailoring, a seamless knit, an elevated terrace, a game's realm. So
  does the client's own name (Elevate Pilates) where the logo, the title before its ":" or
  `og:site_name` writes it: one WARN [copy-brand-word], kept when the brief gives the name.
- **Stock lines** [copy-stock-phrase]: "In today's fast-paced world", "Unlock the power of", "The
  future of X is here", "Say goodbye to", "Whether you're A or B", "Join thousands of", "Trusted by teams
  worldwide", "Imagine a world where", "Ready to transform your X?", "Look no further", "one-stop shop",
  "X made simple", "at your fingertips", "in just a few clicks", "It's not just a X, it's a Y", "Not
  only X but also Y", "Here's the thing", "Let that sink in".
- **Residue** [copy-residue]: "Certainly!", "I hope this helps", "[Company Name]", lorem ipsum,
  `{{tokens}}`, markdown asterisks or `##` on the rendered page, a `[NEED]` left in. The strongest single
  tell: a conversation or a template pasted into the page.
- **Shapes:** the -ing rider tacked onto a fact (", ensuring a smooth start") [copy-ing-rider]; the
  question answered at once ("The result? Three hours back.") and the colon reveal ("One thing changed:
  X") [copy-reveal]; "serves as", "stands as", "plays a key role" where "is" or "has" would do
  [copy-puffery].
- **Punctuation:** em dashes everywhere [copy-em-dash]; exclamation marks in body copy
  [copy-exclaim]; emoji as bullets; an arrow after each link's words, whatever the link.
- **Dead metaphors:** landscape, ecosystem, journey (unless it is travel), "in the X space", hub,
  "the world of", "where X meets Y", "in the heart of" [copy-puffery]. Name the street or the thing.

## Second generation: the tells now

These look like good copy, which is why they survive review.

- **The house voice** (the meta tell). Warm, wry, modest, a little literary, for every client. Fix:
  a register from `copy-registers.md`, chosen per client.
- **Invented specifics** (ban). "6:12 a.m., from the window of Room 9", "Batch No. 047", "38% fewer
  re-runs": detail produced as decoration because detail persuades. Fix: the brief's details only;
  without them, a plainer line.
- **The strip of figures** [copy-stat-strip]. A row of three or four figures, each over a one-word
  label, under the hero or the story, on nearly every model page. Fix: each number in the sentence it proves; a strip only
  of plain facts the brief gives (a price, the hours, a count). A menu's prices, a timetable and a column
  of one unit are not strips.
- **Two-fragment headings "X. Y."** (cap 1) [copy-two-fragment]. "Twelve rooms. Three ways to stay."
  Fix: the other heading shapes in `copy-moves.md`: a name with a claim under it, a verb and the thing,
  a plain sentence.
- **Number-pair headings** (cap 0 to 1) [copy-number-pair]. "Four projects, four very different
  problems." Two unrelated model pages wrote almost exactly this. Fix: say what the section holds.
- **Contrast frames and their substitutes** (cap 2 in all) [copy-contrast]. "Freshness isn't a
  slogan here." Suppress "not X but Y" and it returns as "rather than", "instead of", "without the".
  Fix: state the positive fact alone. A buyer's question in the FAQ is not the device.
- **Negation runs** (cap 1) [copy-negation]. "No forms, no back-and-forth." Keep one only when each
  item is a refusal the buyer can check.
- **Virtue words** (ban about ourselves) [copy-virtue]. honest, calm, quiet, actually, genuinely,
  truly, simply, thoughtful, carefully, intentional, steady, dependable. Fix: show it with an admission
  or a fact. A page never calls itself honest.
- **The dry closer.** "They hold spoons now." on the end of most paragraphs; the same joke on two
  unrelated sites. Fix: end on information; the humour moves to the microcopy.
- **The footer sign-off** [copy-footer-signoff]. "Made in Rotterdam, fired at 1,260 degrees."
  "Every Tuesday since 2019." Fix: the legal row of `copy.md`, nothing else.
- **The name's metaphor run into the ground.** A brand called Kiln that "fires" every section. Fix:
  once, or never.
- **The origin template.** "In [year], [two first names] found [an old hardware store] and kept [one
  original detail]." Fix: the brief's real story; with none, no story section.
- **Polished testimonials** [copy-quotes]. Always three, each a small story with a number and a
  punchline. On a tasteskill page there are none unless the brief gives them, word for word.
- **The default cast** [copy-cast, copy-cast-company]. People: Priya (Raman, Shah, Nair), Daniel or
  Amara Okafor, Marcus, Dana, Aisha, Lena M., Tomas, Nora, Maya, Mara and Theo, Isla, Ines, Jess, Sarah J.,
  Elara. Companies: Fieldnote, Kestrel, Halcyon, Brightloop, Acme, Northwind, Lumen, Nimbus, Apex, Zenith,
  Vertex. Fix: person names only from the brief; a mock's names fit its town and generation; a coined
  brand is none of these (`copy.md`, names.json).
- **The section template.** Eyebrow, claim heading, short lede, three or four cards, every section;
  "Kind words" over the quotes; step numbers on parallel features [copy-numbered]; a small label set
  over each section's heading [copy-eyebrows]; "Most popular" on the middle plan. Fix: shape from the reader's questions
  (`copy-voice.md` section 3).
- **Response-time promises** [copy-response-time]. "Within two working days" on site after site. Fix:
  one, from the brief, worded the same wherever it repeats.
- **"Since [year]"** [copy-since]: once, where it matters, from the brief.
- **Proof figures** [copy-proof-figure]. "3x faster", "10,000+ teams", "98% satisfied": round, neat
  and unsourced. Fix: only figures the brief gives, with their unit, in a sentence.
- **Perfect evenness.** Every card the same length, every paragraph the same arc [copy-rhythm]. Fix:
  spend words where the brief knows most; one section may run long, one may be two lines.
- **Microcopy left unwritten.** A hand-tuned hero over a stock form error and a stock thank-you. Fix:
  write them in the register (`copy-moves.md`).
- **Process talk** [copy-reveal]. "This section shows", "Below, you'll find", "Here are 3 reasons",
  "We've added". The page never talks about itself or about how it was built.
- **The stale year** [copy-stale-year]. A copyright line older than this year.

## Over-correction: what the rules themselves produce

| Rule applied | Habit it breeds | Counter |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No em dashes | Comma splices, full stops only | colons, brackets, semicolons where natural |
| No "not X but Y" | "rather than", "instead of", "without the" | count them together; state the positive |
| No hype words | calm vocabulary: quietly, steady, honest, practical | a fact in place of any adjective |
| Avoid threes | everything in pairs | list as many items as there are |
| Be specific | invented numbers and anecdotes | the fact sheet, or a plainer line |
| Short, punchy sentences | a drumbeat of fragments | one sentence a section may run long |
| End strong | a moral or a quip on every paragraph | end on information |
| Add personality | a joke in every section | a humour budget, spent in the microcopy |
| Vary section length | one huge and one tiny section on every page | length follows the material |
| One rule pack on every page | a new uniform house style | the sameness check across pages |

## Not tells (leave them alone)

Perfect grammar. Plain "is" and "has". "In order to". A transition word on its own. Title case when it
is the client's house style. One "no card needed" when it is true. A narrow superlative the brief can
prove. A refrain repeated on purpose. A list of three when there are three things. Copy the client wrote
